common_name: Beauty Kim Prayer Plant (Variegated Rabbit's Foot Maranta)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, peat-based potting mix; Beauty Kim wants high humidity and consistent moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.

directions: Beauty Kim is a variegated sport of the classic rabbit's foot prayer plant, overlaying the usual rows of dark olive blotches with irregular splashes and streaks of creamy white to pale yellow across the oval leaves, giving each leaf a mottled, hand-painted look distinct from the solid-green kerchoveana form. Because the white sectors carry no chlorophyll, this cultivar needs slightly brighter indirect light than plain rabbit's foot to keep its energy up, though direct sun will still scorch the pale variegated patches. Like other Maranta leuconeura forms it performs a daily nyctinastic leaf movement, folding upward at night and relaxing flat again by day. Keep the peat-based mix consistently moist but not soggy, provide elevated humidity to prevent crisping along the delicate white leaf margins, and divide congested clumps in spring, keeping a mix of variegated and green growing points on each division since the variegation can occasionally revert.
sources: Specialty houseplant nursery listings (Maranta leuconeura kerchoveana variegata trade name)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Mohler is partially self-fertile and will set a light crop alone, but fruiting is heavier and more reliable when a male seedling or another American persimmon is planted nearby for pollination.

directions: Mohler is a named American persimmon selection distributed through the efforts of pomologist Lee Reich of New Paltz, New York, and valued chiefly for ripening unusually early even in cool northern climates, with fruit coloring and softening by late August to early September rather than after the first hard frosts typical of the species. The glowing deep-orange fruit develops rich, sweet flavor once fully soft, while unripe fruit remains strongly astringent like all Diospyros virginiana. The tree responds well to pruning to keep it in a manageable 15-25 foot range for home orchards, and it produces vivid orange and yellow fall foliage color in addition to its fruit crop. Mohler is a useful choice for gardeners in shorter-season or colder regions (zones 5-9) who want an American persimmon that reliably finishes ripening before autumn frosts arrive.
sources: One Green World Nursery — Mohler American Persimmon variety notes
Cricket Hill Garden — Diospyros 'Mohler' American Persimmon
Whiffletree Farm & Nursery — Mohler Persimmon cultivar description

planting.note: Sow seed in a nursery bed or trays in early to mid summer for bloom the following year, since Alba is a true biennial rather than a first-year-flowering strain; overwinter young rosettes in a sheltered spot before transplanting to final positions in spring.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun where summers are cool. Alba is the classic pure-white-flowered selection of common foxglove, bearing tall spikes of unspotted, ghostly white, pendant bells that glow in the evening border and combine easily with almost any color scheme, unlike the maroon-throated spotting typical of the species. Being a true biennial, it forms only a rosette of foliage the first year and flowers the second before setting seed and dying, so stagger sowings in successive years to keep a continuous supply of blooms; it self-sows reliably where happy, though some seedlings may revert toward purple-flowered types over generations. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site away from children and pets.

planting.note: Sow seed in a nursery bed or trays in early to mid summer for flowering the following year, since this is an old-fashioned biennial strain rather than a first-year-blooming hybrid; grow on young plants over winter before setting out in their final spring positions.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil in partial shade. Sutton's Apricot is a long-grown English heirloom strain of common foxglove, raised by Suttons Seeds, producing tall spikes of soft peachy-apricot bells that are essentially unspotted inside, giving the flower spikes a warmer, gentler glow than the heavily freckled purple-flowered species. Like other seed-grown biennial foxgloves it forms a rosette the first year and blooms the second, and it self-sows readily, though color can drift over generations if grown near other foxglove strains and needs periodic reselection or isolation to stay true to type. All parts are toxic if ingested, so site away from children and pets.

common_name: Glittering Prizes Foxglove (Large-Flowered Spotted Mixed-Color Foxglove)

planting.note: Sow seed in a nursery bed or trays in early to mid summer for flowering the following year; Glittering Prizes is a traditional biennial strain selected for extra-large, heavily marked flowers rather than a first-year-flowering hybrid, so give plants a full season to establish before their spring bloom.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun where summers are cool. Glittering Prizes is a Thompson & Morgan-bred strain of common foxglove selected for unusually large, wide-mouthed bells in a mix of purple, pink, cream, and white, each heavily decorated inside with bold maroon spotting on a pale ground that gives the spikes their glittering, jewel-like effect. As a true biennial it produces only a foliage rosette the first year, flowering densely from the base to the tip of the spike the second, and self-sows readily to maintain a colony once established. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so plant away from areas frequented by children or pets.

common_name: Gelber Herold Rusty Foxglove (Yellow Herald Compact Rusty Foxglove)

planting.note: Sow seed on the surface of moist soil in fall or early spring — seed needs light to germinate and should not be covered. Gelber Herold (German for 'Yellow Herald') is a shorter, earlier-flowering selection of rusty foxglove bred for more reliable garden performance than seed-grown species plants.

directions: Sow on the surface of humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; Gelber Herold is a German-raised selection of rusty foxglove bred more compact and floriferous than the wild species, with densely packed spikes of small, warm honey-yellow bells finely netted with darker veining inside the throat. Its shorter, sturdier habit needs less staking than tall species-grown rusty foxglove while keeping the same refined, architectural spike form prized in mixed borders. Like the species it behaves as a short-lived perennial, persisting a few years and self-sowing lightly to maintain a planting. All parts are toxic if ingested, so site away from children and pets.

common_name: Antioch Hosta (Wavy Green Hosta with Wide Cream-White Margin)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Antioch holds its wide cream-white margin best out of intense afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, avoiding hot midday sun that can scorch the wide creamy margin. Antioch is a long-cultivated Hosta fortunei selection with medium-sized, gently wavy, olive-green leaves bordered by a broad, irregular band of creamy white that ages to pure white as the season progresses. Pale lavender flowers rise on tall scapes in mid to late summer above the mounded, vigorous clump. A dependable, long-established garden-center staple, it multiplies steadily and works well as a bold accent or border planting in shaded beds.

common_name: Kabitan Hosta (Narrow Chartreuse-Gold Hosta with Green Margin)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; some morning sun brightens Kabitan's gold color without scorching the narrow leaves.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some morning sun to intensify leaf color, sheltering from hot afternoon exposure. Kabitan is a compact, fast-spreading hosta selection of Hosta sieboldii with narrow, lance-shaped, wavy-margined leaves that emerge bright chartreuse-gold with a thin dark green edge, forming a low, dense groundcover mound. Pale purple, narrowly funnel-shaped flowers with darker stripes appear on slender scapes in late summer. Its small scale and vivid color make it a popular choice for edging shaded borders, rock gardens, and containers.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Zounds needs some shade to prevent its thick gold leaves from bleaching or scorching.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, protecting from intense afternoon sun that can bleach or scorch the thick gold foliage. Zounds produces heavily corrugated, puckered, cupped leaves in a deep, glowing gold that holds its color well into summer, forming a substantial, dense mound of thick-textured foliage prized for its dramatic surface texture. Near-white flowers appear on stout scapes in summer, though the plant is grown primarily for its bold foliage effect. A long-time favorite for adding strong gold color and textural contrast to shaded borders.

common_name: Fortunei Aureomarginata Hosta (Green Leaf with Gold Margin)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Aureomarginata tolerates a bit more morning sun than many hostas once established.

directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, though it tolerates brief morning sun better than many hostas once established. One of the oldest and most widely planted Hosta fortunei selections, Aureomarginata bears smooth, medium-green, heart-shaped leaves edged in a broad, irregular band of gold that ages to creamy yellow as the season progresses. Pale lavender, funnel-shaped flowers rise on tall scapes in midsummer. A classic, dependable garden-center staple valued for its vigor, adaptability, and long garden history.
